plan: Complete enhanced-ACT social-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000037, 'The Day of Two Noons'), about 600 words, on the railroads' 1883 adoption of standard time and the author's argument that noon became a convention. Topic checked against every ACT Reading passage opening and all verbal banks (no time-zone or railroad-time passage). 9 questions, 4 aimed at applying or reconstructing reasoning (direction of solar time, two noons, partial concession, applying the final claim).

passages.title: The Day of Two Noons
passages.text:
In the middle of the nineteenth century, it was noon in an American town when the sun stood highest over it. Because the sun appears to move westward across the sky by one degree of longitude about every four minutes, noon in Boston came several minutes before noon in New York, and noon in Chicago came well after both. For most of history, the difference had hardly mattered. A farmer had no need to know what time it was a hundred miles away, and a traveler on horseback could simply adjust a watch along the road.

The railroads changed that. A train that left one city on its local time and arrived in another on a different local time produced schedules that were hard to read and, on single-track lines where trains running in opposite directions had to meet and pass at sidings, dangerous to get wrong. Each railroad solved the problem for itself by running on the time of a chosen city, often the one where it had its headquarters, so that by the early 1880s the nation's railroads were using dozens of different times. A traveler changing trains at a large station might find several clocks on the wall, each correct for some line and none correct for the street outside.

In 1883, after years of proposals, the railroads' own association agreed on a simpler system. The country would be divided into four broad zones, each keeping the mean time of a single meridian, so that clocks in neighboring zones would differ by exactly one hour. On Sunday, November 18, telegraph signals coordinated the change, and railroad clocks across the country were reset. In towns east of their zone's central meridian, where local noon had already passed, clocks were turned back several minutes, and noon arrived a second time; newspapers called it the Day of Two Noons.

What is striking is who made the change. No act of Congress required it; the federal government did not make standard time law until 1918. The railroads simply announced a schedule, and because so much of daily life now ran on train times, much of the public followed. Many cities adjusted their own clocks within weeks. Others resisted, some for years, and objectors complained that the railroads had no right to decide what time it was. They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority at all. They had something more effective, which was a network that everyone else needed to use.

The episode is often told as a story about technology, and in part it is. But the deeper change was in what people understood time to be. For a town that kept local time, noon was a fact about the sky, which anyone could check by watching a shadow. Under standard time, noon became an agreement, correct only because enough people had decided to keep it. The sun did not move, and no one was asked to stop watching it. What moved was the authority to say what time it was, from the sky to the timetable.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Congress created standard time zones to make train travel in the United States safer.
choices.B: Railroads made the hour a shared convention rather than a local reading of the sun.
choices.C: Railroad schedules in the 1800s were confusing because trains often ran late.
choices.D: Most Americans refused to accept standard time until the federal government required it.

candidates.explanation: The passage traces how railroads, without legal authority, replaced local solar time with a few standard zones, and argues that this turned noon from 'a fact about the sky' into 'an agreement.'

A.rationale: The passage says no act of Congress required the change until 1918.

C.rationale: Confusion came from many different times, not from late trains.

D.rationale: Much of the public followed within weeks; only some resisted.

hints: What does the last paragraph say really changed?

strategy.explanation: Combine the history with the final paragraph's point.

candidates.remember: In a history passage, the main idea often includes the author's interpretation.

candidates.stem: Based on the first paragraph, a town located well west of Chicago that kept local time would have reached noon:

choices.B: at the same moment as Chicago.
choices.C: at the same moment as Boston.

candidates.evidence: noon in Chicago came well after both
candidates.explanation: The sun appears to move westward, so places farther west reach noon later: Boston, then New York, then Chicago. A town west of Chicago would reach noon later still.

A.rationale: The sun moves westward, so it reaches western towns later, not earlier.

B.rationale: Different longitudes reach the sun's highest point at different moments.

C.rationale: Boston is far east of Chicago and reaches noon earliest of the three.

hints: Which way does the sun appear to move?
candidates.remember: Apply the passage's rule to a case it does not mention.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must extend the stated pattern to a new place; 'earlier' tempts readers who reverse the direction.

candidates.stem: The description of a station with "several clocks on the wall" (paragraph 2) mainly illustrates:

choices.A: the confusion that arose when each railroad kept its own time.
choices.B: the high cost of building large railroad stations.
choices.C: the railroads' success in agreeing on a single time.
choices.D: travelers' preference for local time over railroad time.

candidates.evidence: each correct for some line and none correct for the street outside
candidates.explanation: Several clocks, each right for one railroad and none for the town, show the confusion of dozens of separate railroad times before 1883.

C.rationale: At this point the railroads had not yet agreed; that came in 1883.

D.rationale: The detail shows conflicting clocks, not anyone's preference.

hints: When does this detail take place, before or after 1883?

strategy.explanation: Place the detail in the timeline.

candidates.remember: Concrete details often illustrate the problem a passage then solves.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that mismatched times were especially dangerous on single-track lines because:

choices.A: single-track lines ran through more towns than other lines did.
choices.B: trains on single-track lines traveled faster than other trains did.
choices.C: opposing trains had to meet at set places at set times.
choices.D: single-track lines were owned by several railroads at once.

candidates.evidence: trains running in opposite directions had to meet and pass at sidings
candidates.explanation: On one track, opposing trains must wait for each other at sidings at scheduled times; if two crews read different times, they could meet on the same track.

A.rationale: The passage does not compare how many towns the lines served.

D.rationale: Ownership of the track is not mentioned.

hints: How do two trains pass each other on one track?
candidates.remember: Infer the risk from the specific arrangement the passage describes.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, some towns experienced "two noons" on November 18, 1883, because:

choices.A: their clocks, already past local noon, were set back to noon by the new standard.
choices.B: their clocks were set forward, so noon came earlier than it usually did.
choices.C: they kept local time and standard time on separate clocks all day long.
choices.D: the telegraph signal that set the clocks arrived twice on some lines.

candidates.evidence: where local noon had already passed, clocks were turned back several minutes
candidates.explanation: In towns east of their zone's meridian, local noon came first; then the clocks were turned back several minutes to match standard time, so they reached noon a second time.

B.rationale: Clocks were set back, not forward, in the towns that saw two noons.

C.rationale: The passage describes a single reset, not two clocks running all day.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the signal arrived twice.

hints: Were the clocks set forward or back, and when?

strategy.explanation: Read the last sentence of paragraph 3 closely.

candidates.remember: Track the order of events to explain a surprising result.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must reconstruct the sequence (local noon, then a reset backward); the 'set forward' choice reverses it.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 4, the author's attitude toward the objectors is best described as:

choices.A: dismissive, because the objectors had misunderstood the law.
choices.B: fully supportive, because the change should have waited for Congress.
choices.C: indifferent, because the objectors had little effect on the change.
choices.D: granting their legal point but not that it explained the change.

candidates.evidence: They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority at all.
candidates.explanation: The author concedes the railroads lacked legal authority but adds that they had 'something more effective,' the network everyone needed, so the objection did not explain or stop the change.

A.rationale: The author says they were 'in a sense, correct' about the law.

B.rationale: The author never says the change should have waited.

C.rationale: The author engages with their claim rather than ignoring it.

hints: What does the author grant, and what does the author add?

strategy.explanation: Read both sentences after 'They were, in a sense, correct.'

candidates.remember: A concession followed by 'but' or a contrast usually limits the point conceded.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must read a partial concession; the 'dismissive' choice ignores 'in a sense, correct.'

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "striking" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: What is striking is who made the change.
candidates.explanation: The author points out something remarkable: the change came from railroads, not government. 'Striking' means notable here.

A.rationale: 'Striking' can mean hitting hard, but here it describes something worth noticing.

B.rationale: 'Striking' can describe good looks, but not in this sentence.

D.rationale: Nothing in the sentence concerns speed.

hints: Why does the author call attention to who made the change?
candidates.remember: Several familiar meanings can be wrong; test each in the sentence.

candidates.subskill: Applying an idea to a new situation
candidates.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the change in the meaning of noon described in the last paragraph?

choices.A: A farmer watches a shadow to decide when noon has come.
choices.B: A town's clocks read noon before the sun reaches its highest point.
choices.C: A traveler finds two station clocks that disagree by several minutes.
choices.D: A city passes a law requiring its clocks to match the position of the sun.

candidates.evidence: noon became an agreement, correct only because enough people had decided to keep it
candidates.explanation: Under standard time, noon is whatever the agreed clocks say, even when the sun disagrees. A clock reading noon before the sun's highest point shows that noon is now set by agreement.

A.rationale: This is the old way, in which noon is 'a fact about the sky.'

C.rationale: This describes the confusion before standard time, not the new meaning.

D.rationale: This would return noon to the sky, the opposite of the change.

hints: Under standard time, what makes noon 'correct'?

strategy.explanation: Sort the choices into old meaning, confusion and new meaning.

candidates.remember: To apply an idea, find the case that could happen only under the new idea.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must translate an abstract claim into a concrete case; the shadow choice tempts readers who pick the familiar picture of noon.

candidates.subskill: Purpose of a fact in an argument
candidates.stem: The fact that "the federal government did not make standard time law until 1918" (paragraph 4) mainly supports the author's point that:

choices.A: standard time spread by practice long before a law required it.
choices.B: the railroads opposed every attempt to make standard time a law.
choices.C: most American cities refused to change their clocks until 1918.
choices.D: the four time zones were redrawn when the law was finally passed.

candidates.evidence: No act of Congress required it
candidates.explanation: The thirty-five-year gap between the 1883 change and the 1918 law shows that the public adopted standard time because of the railroads' schedules, not because of law.

B.rationale: Nothing says the railroads opposed a law.

D.rationale: The passage does not mention any redrawing.

strategy.explanation: Ask what the gap in dates proves.

candidates.remember: A date can serve as evidence when the gap it reveals matters.
